Figure 10: Baseline HP System Model: Verification of Rated Cooling Mode Predictions Using quasi-steady-state approaches, ORNL conducted a set of parametric studies to investigate the potential of the defined targets (5 tons, 4-hour peak load shift) across different United States climate zones. The approach was to examine the demand- reduction potential of HP-TES in 8 selected cities for each US climate zone (Table 7). Thus, simulations of the PCM-HP and DX baseline systems were conducted using weather data for the summer and winter design days. The indoor hourly conditions were obtained using EnergyPlus to calculate the building load for a 2200 ft2 single-family house built in accordance with the 2006 International Energy Conservation Code (IECC) [75]. Using varying UA and PCM materials, the models simulated quasi-steady-state conditions to investigate demand reduction during peak hours. Balancing between heating and cooling demand reductions of 50%, it was found that selecting the higher temperature PCM (25°C) would increase heating demand reductions given the lower temperature lifts (i.e., higher evaporating pressures & temperatures), and the lower temperature PCM (18.5°C) in cooling mode, corresponding to lower discharge pressures and temperatures. Consequently, the selection of the PCM temperature should balance both heating and cooling, and a 22°C PCM temperature would provide a suitable demand reduction for the design day in both modes. Figure 11: TES battery sizes over a wide range of PCM temperatures The design-day simulations for different climate zones differ, depending on whether the location is cooling-dominated or heating-dominated (Figure 12). In cooling-dominated regions (Riverside, CA), a lower-temperature PCM can achieve higher demand reduction, Page 21 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park specifically 30–50%. This reduction decreases as the PCM temperature increases, as pressure and temperature lifts grow. Conversely, higher demand reductions can be achieved in heating mode for cold-climate zones, as the PCM raises evaporating conditions, providing complete cooling capacity at lower compressor power and without backup heating.
